analysis.one_liner: Charges royalties and cleanup bonds on hardrock mining of federal land and ends below-market claim sales.
analysis.headline: The House passed hardrock mining reform 316–108 and the Senate passed its own version, but the conference committee never agreed, so mining of federal land stayed royalty-free under the 1872 law.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Mining Law of 1872, anyone who staked a claim on federal land could mine gold, silver, and copper without paying the government anything, and could buy the land itself outright for a token price. This bill would have charged an 8% royalty on production from new claims, required annual claim fees, forced miners to get permits, post cleanup bonds, and reclaim the land, and created a fund to clean up thousands of abandoned mines that still pollute western water. It passed the House by a wide bipartisan margin and cleared the Senate, but the two versions were never reconciled and the bill died.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would finally get a share of the value of minerals taken from public land; western communities whose water and land are polluted by unreclaimed mines; and anyone who uses public lands damaged by a century of unregulated mining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and western communities near mines

how_it_helps.text: Sets a minimum royalty of 8% of gross income on production of locatable minerals from claims located under the Act, payable to the United States.
Requires $25 location fees and annual claim maintenance fees of $100–$200 per claim, with the money deposited into a new abandoned-mine reclamation fund.

Requires permits for any mining that disturbs the surface, with approved reclamation plans, financial assurance bonds covering the full cost of reclamation including long-term water treatment, and quarterly-style inspections with civil penalties and citizen suits to enforce compliance.

Prohibits issuance of mining patents after January 5, 1993 unless new administrative requirements are met, targeting the practice the bill's own findings describe as transferring mineral-rich public land to private ownership below fair market value.
Creates an Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund, administered by Interior, to restore land and water damaged by past mining, with grants to eligible states.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, who would pay royalties, annual fees, permitting costs, and full reclamation bonds. Opponents argued these costs would reduce mining employment, though their attempt to force a no-net-job-loss guarantee was rejected on the floor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: Opponents warned that royalties, fees, and permits would raise costs enough to cause net job losses in mining and push production overseas; a Republican motion to recommit demanding an Interior-model guarantee of no net job losses failed 148–270, so the concern was debated but never proven or resolved.

The two chambers passed materially different bills: the Senate struck the House text and substituted the language of S. 775, which uses different fee and royalty structures and a Royalty Review Commission to study royalty effects, leaving the actual charge on the industry unsettled.

Permit and bonding requirements add administrative burden for all operators, though the bill waives annual maintenance fees for holders of ten or fewer claims and reduces fees for holders of fewer than 50 claims in the Senate version, concentrating costs on large companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public case is strong: for over a century the government collected nothing for minerals worth billions and left the cleanup bills to taxpayers, and the bill's own findings say the 1872 law no longer serves the public interest. The costs fall on one concentrated industry, and the bill includes transition protections and small-claimant waivers. The unproven job-loss objection was the opposition's main argument, and the House rejected it when given the chance.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed versions—the House 316–108, the Senate its own substitute by voice vote—but the conference committee appointed in May 1994 met once in June and never produced a merged bill, so reform died when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 5, 1993 and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, which reported an amended bill on a 28–14 vote.
On November 18, 1993 the House passed the bill 316–108: 245 of 257 voting Democrats and 70 of 175 voting Republicans in favor.
A Republican motion to recommit with instructions to guarantee no net job losses under Interior's economic models failed 148–270 the same day.
On November 22, 1993 the Senate struck all of the House text, substituted the language of S. 775, and passed it by voice vote, then insisted on its amendment and asked for a conference.
The House agreed to a conference in May 1994 and conferees from five committees were appointed; the conference met on June 29, 1994 and never reported an agreement.
Congress ended January 3, 1995 with no law, leaving the 1872 Mining Law and its royalty-free treatment of federal hardrock minerals unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: the 1872 Mining Law stayed in place, so mining of federal gold, silver, and copper remained royalty-free and claim land could still be patented for token prices. Taxpayers collected nothing from public minerals and no dedicated fund was created to clean up abandoned mines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

sides.party_line_note: House passage was bipartisan in count—245 of 257 Democrats and 70 of 175 Republicans voted yes—but 137 of 175 Republicans backed the job-loss motion to recommit, and the conference that failed to agree included mining-state senators of both parties.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper on federal land)
industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's core deal under the 1872 law: paying no royalty on minerals taken from public land and buying claim land for token prices. Its gain under the status quo came directly from what the bill would have charged the public for.

Annual maintenance fees are waived for holders of ten or fewer claims, but new permit, reclamation, and bonding requirements apply to operations of all sizes, and permit costs fall relatively harder on small operators.

industries.industry: Reclamation, bonding, and environmental consulting services
industries.note: Mandatory reclamation bonds, monitoring, and a new abandoned-mine cleanup fund would create a large stream of cleanup and assurance work paid for by operators and the new fund.
States would receive reclamation grants from the new fund and a share of receipts under the Senate version, addressing abandoned mines that threaten state water and land.
